BoTtOm-Up PaRsInG
• Bottom-up parsing is more general than top-down parsing
 
– And just as efficient
 
– Builds on ideas in top-down parsing
 
– Preferred method in practice
• Also called LR parsing
 
– L means that tokens are read left to right
 
– R means that it constructs a rightmost derivation ! 
3

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-1-47.pdf
pages.text:
An Introductory Example 
• LR parsers don’t need left-factored grammars and can also handle left-recursive grammars
• Consider the following grammar:   E → E + ( E ) | int
 
– Why is this not LL(1)?    
 
 
An expression (E) can be: Another expression followed by + ( E ), or Just an int.
 
 
 
Here, E → E + ( E ) is left-recursive, so LL(1) fails.
An LL(1) parser would check when it sees the first int:
•
Should it expand E → int or try E → E + (E)?
•
With only 1 symbol lookahead, it cannot decide.
An LR parser doesn’t guess.
•
It shifts int,   then reduces it to E,
•
then when it sees + ( int ) ..., it recognizes the pattern E + ( E ) and reduces correctly.
•
Finally, it parses the whole input without problems.
Consider the string: 
 
 
int + ( int ) + ( int )

• str w input string of terminals 
• Repeat
• Identify β in str such that A →β is a production (i.e., str = αβγ) 
• Replace β by A in str (i.e., str w = α A γ)
• until str = S (the start symbol)

Important Fact #1 
• Important Fact #1 about bottom-up parsing:
 
 
An LR parser traces a rightmost derivation in reverse 
14

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-1-47.pdf
pages.text:
Where Do Reductions Happen 
• Important Fact #1 has an interesting consequence:
 
– Let αβγ be a step of a bottom-up parse
 
– Assume the next reduction is by using A→ β
 
– Then γ is a string of terminals
• Why? Because αAγ → αβγ is a step in a rightmost derivation 
15

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-1-47.pdf
pages.text:
Idea: Notation
• Split string into two substrings
 – Right substring is as yet unexamined by parsing (a string of terminals)
 – Left substring has terminals and non-terminals
• The dividing point is marked by a I
 – The I is not part of the string
• Initially, all input is unexamined: Ix1, x2, . . . xn 
16
